decisions.quote: AbstractThis article evaluates the conceptual replication of a text and audio Behavioral Change Communication Program (Crianza Positiva) on parenting practices and well-being in households with children aged 0–2 years in Uruguay during the COVID-19 pandemic. The intervention uses behavioral economics tools to reorient parents’ attention towards positive parenting practices. Using an experimental design involving 39 early childhood centers (687 families), we find no effects of the intervention on the outcomes of interest. This finding contrasts with those found in a previous edition of the program in 2018, which showed improvements in parental involvement, in the quality of parent–child interaction, and in adult–child language patterns (Balsa in Child & Youth Care Forum 53:1–22, 2023a; Balsa in Behavioural Public Policy 7: 607–643, 2023c; Bloomfield in Review of the Economics of the Household 21:95–130, 2023). decisions.reason: The current study (Balsa, Bloomfield, & Cid, 2024/2025) evaluates the 2020 COVID-19 Crianza Positiva e-messaging RCT (N = 687: 348 treatment, 339 control across 39 CAIF centers, without prior workshops) and contrasts its null results with three 2018-edition papers: Balsa et al. (2023a), Balsa et al. (2023c), and Bloomfield et al. (2022/2023, shipped row 1498). Component verification confirms Balsa et al. (2023a) is a distinct 3-arm study (N = 759 across 27 centers: Workshop+SMS, Workshop-only, Control; N = 442 free-play videos) whose primary positive effects were on blind-coded observational PICCOLO parent-child interaction quality, whereas shipped row 1498 evaluates the 24-center e-messaging RCT (N = 529) on caregiver self-reports (Cabrera activities, E2P positive-parenting subset, PSI dysfunctional interaction, knowledge, PSOC). In the current study, English Footnote 8 explicitly notes the absence of observational data, and the 9-page 2022 Spanish IDB brief (IDB-DP-00987) lists telephone/web self-reports (Cabrera, E2P relational subscale, PCCTS, 10 belief items, co-parenting, PSI, CES-D) while comparing only Cabrera, knowledge, and PSI in Figure 3. Because the full English journal body (Methods, Results, and tables) remains unavailable, we cannot determine whether Balsa et al. (2023a)'s interaction-quality findings are conceptually retested via self-report proxies beyond shipped row 1498.

decisions.reason: Component verification confirms Balsa et al. (2023c) shares the 2018 24-center e-messaging RCT (N = 529, AEARCTR-0003585) with Bloomfield et al. (2022/2023, shipped row 1498) but tests distinct primary endpoints: automated voice-type classifier acoustic features from 10-minute free-play videos (N = 317 follow-up; core longitudinal N = 157–159, finding increased adult pitch range +0.424 ERB and non-robust vocalization duration changes) plus secondary self-report literacy items (reading, telling stories, singing, counting) overlapping Cabrera didactic activities in shipped row 1498. Although the current English abstract cites Balsa et al. (2023c) regarding improvements in adult-child language patterns and the 2022 Spanish IDB brief states the trial sought to evaluate language-stimulation practices, English Footnote 8 explicitly confirms the absence of observational data, and the Spanish brief lists no acoustic or standalone adult-child language-pattern measure beyond the general Cabrera parental involvement index. Because the full English journal article body (Methods, Results, and tables) is unavailable, we cannot verify whether the published English article reports any conceptual retest of Balsa et al. (2023c)'s adult-child language endpoints distinct from the self-report parental investment items already represented by shipped row 1498.
